## The senses, more than five
kind: visual
The senses bring the world in, and the body organizes it to answer (sensory integration). Two quiet senses join the five we name. (from Beyond Discipline)

### The five we name
**What it is.** Sight (visual), touch (tactile), hearing (auditory), taste and smell. The ones we name with children.
**What it does for a child.** When the organizing goes smoothly, a child can pay attention, learn, plan a movement, be with friends and manage feelings.

### Balance and movement (vestibular)
**What it is.** The inner ear tells a child where their head is in space and how fast they are moving.
**What it does for a child.** A foundation for the rest. When it comes in confused, what we see on the floor is behavior.

### Body sense (proprioception)
**What it is.** Receptors in the joints, muscles and tendons tell a child where each limb is and how much force to use.
**What it does for a child.** A child who hugs too hard, crashes into friends or cannot tell they were bumped is still building that map.

### Heavy work
**What it is.** Pushing, pulling, carrying, lifting, digging and climbing send strong, steady messages through joints and muscles (proprioceptive input).
**What it does for a child.** Calms and organizes the nervous system and raises attention, for the child who seeks movement and the one who avoids it.

Footer. Adapted from the Early Learning Institute tip sheets by Pat Boblitt and April Davis and from A. Jean Ayres, by way of The senses and the body in Beyond Discipline. Set-ups live in the Idea bank under Heavy work, Obstacle courses, Swinging, spinning and hanging, and Calm body after big movement.

## Six kinds of risk children seek
kind: visual
Six kinds of risk children seek on their own, scared and thrilled at once (scary-funny). Each begins low and rises with readiness. (from Risky Play)

### Great heights
**Where it lives here.** Trees, the climbing structure, spools and crates stacked by children, the top of the hill.
**Lowest to highest.** Low wide planks on the ground, then planks on crates, then high branches.

### High speed
**Where it lives here.** Running down the slope, the tire swing, wagons and wheelbarrows at a run, sliding.
**Lowest to highest.** Slow swings and running in open space and stopping, then faster swings and spinning.

### Dangerous tools
**Where it lives here.** Hammers, saws and drills at the woodworking bench, knives at the cooking table, shovels and rakes.
**Lowest to highest.** Sticks and small hammers beside an adult, then the first saw and drill, then knives.

### Dangerous elements
**Where it lives here.** The creek on walks, the pretend campfire, the hot dehydrator, deep water in the sensory table.
**Lowest to highest.** Rises to fire safety at the pretend campfire and creek walks with water safety certified educators.

### Rough and tumble
**Where it lives here.** Wrestling with agreements, chase, pillow crashes, the big body play of twos and threes.
**Lowest to highest.** The big body play of twos and threes, then chase and wrestling with agreements.

### Disappearing or getting lost
**Where it lives here.** Hiding places, the willow dome, the far corners of the farm, out of sight and still heard.
**Lowest to highest.** Hiding where an adult sees, then out of sight and in earshot, then wider wandering with a plan.

Footer. Adapted from Ellen Sandseter's six kinds of risky play (2007), by way of The six kinds of risky play and How risky play grows in Risky Play. Set-ups live in the Idea bank under Risky play set-ups.

## Who decides what at the table
kind: visual
Ellyn Satter's division of responsibility in feeding. Each side keeps to its own job, and our Meal Time Values are her division almost word for word. (from The Communal Table)

### The adult decides
**The jobs.** What food is offered, when and where. Offers a varied table at steady times, sits down to eat with the child, and does not coax, praise, bargain or restrict.
**How it looks at our table.** We provide the setting, the food and the tools. Courses come in order, water, then vegetables and salad, the most desirable food last. An educator describes the food and eats alongside.

### The child decides
**The jobs.** Whether to eat and how much. Comes to the table, may say no, may eat a lot one day and little the next, and learns to trust their own fullness (self-regulation of intake).
**How it looks at our table.** Each child chooses what and how much. Children serve themselves from bowls at the center, take a fair first serving and come back for more. A new food stays a warm invitation.

Footer. Adapted from Ellyn Satter, Child of Mine (1983), the division of responsibility in feeding, by way of Who decides what in The Communal Table. Set-ups live in the Idea bank under Piazza and culinary atelier and Cooking and food.

## Serve and return
kind: visual
The back and forth between child and adult (serve and return) builds the brain's circuits for language, attention and relationship. (from The Present Educator)

### A serve
**What it looks like.** A child serves with a look, a sound, a gesture or a question, many times a day.
**What the adult does.** Stays close enough to see it. From a base, an educator sees serves a moving adult misses.

### A return
**What it looks like.** The adult notices and answers in a way that fits, and the exchange repeats through ordinary days.
**What the adult does.** Says what they will do first, moves slowly, observes, and lets the child set the pace (Magda Gerber).

### Twos and threes
**What it looks like.** A serve may be a cry, a reach or a storm, and the child borrows steadiness from a nearby adult (co-regulation).
**What the adult does.** A hand offered, a lap, a lowered voice, and staying through the storm.

### Threes and fours
**What it looks like.** Serves come in words and questions, and the child can take in a short answer.
**What the adult does.** Names what is happening and what comes next, with the body still close.

### Fours, fives and TK
**What it looks like.** Children begin to reach for a strategy of their own, a quiet spot, a drink of water, a friend.
**What the adult does.** Stays present, which makes the reaching possible.

Footer. Adapted from the Center on the Developing Child at Harvard and Magda Gerber, by way of Serve and return and Respectful presence in The Present Educator. Set-ups live in the Idea bank under A sitting spot outside and A listening walk.

## Where is a new educator?
kind: visual
Lilian Katz described four stages an educator of young children moves through, each with its own needs. The years are rough. What holds up is the match between stage and support. (from The Educator as Mentor)

### Survival, the first year
**The question.** "Can I get through the day?"
**The support that fits.** On-site support, close by and often, from someone who knows the room, the children and the procedures. Advice from a distance does little.

### Consolidation, the second and third year
**The question.** The educator can run a day and now asks about particular children. "What do I do for the child who leaves every meeting?"
**The support that fits.** A colleague to think with, specific information, and watching the child together.

### Renewal, the third or fourth year
**The question.** The same day done well begins to feel flat. What else is there?
**The support that fits.** New ideas, visits to other programs, conferences, reading and a network beyond the school.

### Maturity, the third to fifth year on
**The question.** The deep questions of the work, about the Image of the Child, the purpose of school and the educator's own growth.
**The support that fits.** Seminars, advanced study and conversation with others at the same point.

Footer. Adapted from Lilian Katz's four stages of educator growth (1972), by way of Where a new educator is in The Educator as Mentor.

## How drawing and writing grow
kind: visual
Two maps of what to look for in a child's marks. The ages are rough, children skip steps, and a child may move back and forth in one week. (from The Class Atelier and The Emergent Writer)

### Twos and threes
**Drawing.** Scribbles of every kind, big arm movement, pleasure in the mark and in watching it appear. Naming comes after making.
**Writing.** Scribbles anywhere on the page, large and circular, with the whole arm. Toward three, marks get named after they are made.

### Threes and fours
**Drawing.** Closed shapes (diagrams), combined shapes and the first suns and people. A story told while drawing, marks named as made.
**Writing.** Scribbles move in lines (directional scribble), letter-like shapes appear, often from the name. The first letter of the name made on purpose.

### Fours, fives and TK
**Drawing.** Drawings planned before the pencil moves (preschematic), with people, animals and places. A drawing can be a plan for building or a map.
**Writing.** Strings of letters, mostly capitals, then groups with spaces. The name nearly right. Labels that match a first sound to a letter, reversals expected.

Footer. Adapted from Rhoda Kellogg and Viktor Lowenfeld on drawing, and Marie Clay and Judith Schickedanz on writing, by way of How drawing grows in The Class Atelier and Stages of writing by age in The Emergent Writer. ## How a child comes to like a food
kind: visual
Tasting many times (repeated exposure) is what moves a child, and pressure works against it. (from Cooking from the Garden and The Communal Table)

### Tasting again
**What the research found.** Liking rose with the number of tastes. Eight to fifteen is an average. Looking did not do it.
**At our table.** A child who refuses kale the first six times is on schedule. A new food stays a warm invitation.

### Wariness of the new (food neophobia)
**What the research found.** Reluctance to taste the unfamiliar is strongest from about two to six. Ordinary, partly inherited, and tasting works on it.
**At our table.** That span is the whole span of our program. A child may explore a new food with every sense before tasting.

### What works against it
**What the research found.** A reward for eating a food lowered liking for it afterward. Restricting a food raised eating of it once available.
**At our table.** No coaxing, praise, bargaining or restricting. Garden food sits beside what the Kitchen planned, and no one is asked to try a bite.

### Watching others
**What the research found.** Preschoolers seated with friends who chose a different vegetable shifted their choice, and it held weeks later. Adults do the same.
**At our table.** Educators sit with children, describe the food and eat alongside them. Children serve themselves from shared bowls.

Footer. Adapted from Leann Birch's studies and Ellyn Satter's division of responsibility, by way of How children learn to like a food in Cooking from the Garden and What Leann Birch found in The Communal Table. Set-ups live in the Idea bank under Cooking and food.
